records.text: Petitioners' claim for injunctive and declaratory relief to enforce the terms of the reimbursement clause in the benefit plan at issue in this case falls squarely within the language of ERISA, section 502(a)(3)(A), which appears in full text at page 13 of our brief, which provides for a civil action by a fiduciary to enjoin any act or practice which violates the terms of the plan.

Well, Your Honor, we believe that the language and the structure and the purpose of ERISA support the proposition that section 502(a)(3)(A), specifically in this case (a)(3)(A), to enjoin the Knudsons from disbursing funds as to which they had power to determine --
In fact, Your Honor, the concept of a constructive trust, which is -- which is employed by many of the lower courts, the courts of appeals, to enforce these reimbursement causes --
Section 404(a) of ERISA obligates fiduciaries to enforce the terms of the plan. It's one of their obligations.

ON BEHALF OF THE UNITED STATES, AS AMICUS CURIAE, SUPPORTING THE PETITIONERS MR. WOLFSON: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: I'd like to start with the point that was being made by my colleague, which is that this is the only mechanism by which a plan can enforce a term of the plan.

QUESTION: So, you say that -- that under this, since it's exclusively Federal causes of action and since the Federal statute does not provide for any legal remedy, that any so-called equitable remedy is available because there is no legal relief.
QUESTION: Yes, because it says enjoin any act, not -- not any failure to act.
QUESTION: It's very odd that you'd have a -- a body of Federal common law that can be applied only in State courts.

I think that the State tort law is the claim -- creates a claim for negligence and any damages caused by that. What subrogation does, which I think ought to be a matter of Federal common law which probably just follows the terms of an ERISA plan, is say that the plan can step into the shoes of the beneficiary's rights under State law.
I think the preemption argument as to the subrogation suit, the ordinary tort suit, is much, much weaker to begin with and therefore doesn't require as -- as strong a -- a response.

In -- in the one reference to -- which I cited in -- in my brief I think at page 27 -- in one of the Senate reports that discusses the immediate predecessor of this provision, there's no general reference to any kind of relief that's necessary to -- to make plans protect all of their rights or vice versa. It's been principally a beneficiary protection statute.
